newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China halts issue of diesel import licences.
newsitem.headline: China halts issue of diesel import licences.

text.p: High diesel stocks aided by rampant smuggling have forced China to stop issuing fresh import licences, Chinese traders said on Thursday.
And the government might keep a tight grip on issuing licences for the rest of the year, they said.

Traders at China's state oil firms said the central government only issued a small batch of diesel import licences for China Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec) in early 1997 and there hasn't been any further issue since.
"Diesel stocks are just too high at the moment. Demand (imports) from China will be very very weak in the second half of the year," a well-placed source with a main Chinese oil importer, said.

"There may not be any import licences in the next two to three months, or even in the fourth quarter," a trader with another state importer said from Beijing, citing high diesel stocks at Chinese refineries and smuggling.

Benchmark diesel prices in Singapore fell this week to $19.80 per barrel, the lowest level in at least three years, but the near-term bottom was still not in sight mainly due to China's absence from the market, Singapore traders said.
"We can hardly sell any of our diesel stocks recently, and the situation is no better in other coastal refineries. Why should we import diesel?" said a source with the southeastern Fujian refinery.

China depleted its diesel stocks in late 1996 when international diesel prices were at five-year highs. It was forced to import some two million tonnes at the end of 1996 to cover the shortage, Chinese traders said.
Imports in 1996 were 4.6 million tonnes and by April 1997 they were running 77 percent ahead of last year.
The late 1996 stock shortage prompted Sinopec to ask refineries to raise diesel production , they said.
China produced 4.037 million tonnes of diesel in May alone, an 11.5 percent rise from the same period a year ago, according to the State Statistics Bureau. 1996 output was 43.25 million tonnes.
"After the adjustment for more diesel and less gasoline, many refineries now have more than enough diesel," said a source with China International United Oil Corp.
The rapid surge in stocks and strong imports in the first half of 1997 also caused a plunge in domestic diesel prices, traders said.

Diesel prices, set by the state at 2,190 yuan (US$264) per tonne at the beginning of this year, have fallen to 1,900 yuan (US$229) or even lower in some coastal provinces, they said. Official demand was equally discouraged by the notorious diesel smuggling along the southeastern coast, traders said.
"A lot of the smuggled oil actually came through customs under disguise such as transshipment but the oil actually went into the domestic markets," a Chinese source said.

In the face of insufficiency at customs to clamp down on such illegal imports, the central government has called for officials in Fujian and Guangdong provinced to Beijing for a meeting last week for countermeasures, the source said.
"But the smuggling problem can not be solved any soon. All I can say is at this moment, diesel is everywhere in China," he said.
